newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe business says it cannot soak fuel prices.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe business says it cannot soak fuel prices.

text.p: Zimbabwe's key private business and industrial sector said on Wednesday it could not absorb a new six to eight percent fuel price rise -- the third this year -- and many companies would pass costs to consumers to stay viable.

Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries (CZI) and Zimbabwe National Chamber of Commerce (ZNCC) also also warned Tuesday's fuel hikes may stoke annual inflation, which fell to a three-year low of 17.7 percent in August on the back of low food prices.

"We are warning consumers to prepare for another round of price increases. There is no way commerce and industry can absorb any further costs, and that includes the fuel prices," said a spokesman at CZI where senior officials are in Europe on an investment promotion drive.

The Zimbabwean government raised the price of petrol and other fuels by between six and eight percent on Tuesday, citing higher operational and procurement costs for its third price increase this year.

"The increases have been necessitated by changes in the FOB (Free On Board) prices that have risen significantly due to recent missile attacks on Iraq by the United States as well as increases in operating costs," Transport and Energy Minister Simon Moyo said, adding industry could easily absorb the fuel increases.
ZNCC president Danny Meyer said many companies were already battling against high input costs to stay viable.
"The minister claims the percentage increase was low and so it should be easily absorbed...That is obviously wishful thinking," he said.

"The business community is already working on reduced margins which cannot be sustained any further by absorbing another increase in input costs. I see this fuel price increase as adding to inflation which has been coming down nicely," he said.

Economic and business consultant John Robertson also said inflation -- which many people were expecting to rise anyway in September and October following consumer price increases in the last few weeks -- could show a steep rise due to the fuel prices.
"If there are no moderating factors, it tends to be that way," he said.
